entries.text: 'Chiefly because they are not the same purchase, and the prices are not substitutes for one another. A certification course buys an IICRC certification, once, through a school approved by the IICRC and its examination. A CARSI course buys a CARSI Southern Hemisphere Restoration Designation and, where that particular course has been approved by the IICRC, credits toward keeping a certification you already hold. Delivery costs differ on top of that: a classroom course carries a venue, an instructor for three days and your travel, and takes you off the tools while it runs. Treat them as two separate line items in a training budget rather than as alternatives to each other.',

"contentBody": "

On the job

A state primary school in Toowoomba, QLD. A leaking box gutter has soaked the wall behind the joinery in two classrooms, and growth is visible when the cupboards come out. A parents' group has heard the words \"toxic mould\" and the principal wants \"air tests before and after\". The insurer's builder rings you and asks whether your company can \"do the clearance testing as well, to keep it simple\".

The idea

On a Level 3 job you will often work beside an independent professional who assesses the building, samples it and decides whether the job has passed. In Australia the person doing that work is most often an occupational hygienist. The Australian Institute of Occupational Hygienists (AIOH) runs a certification program for hygienists, and others hold different science qualifications. Titles vary, so check what the person has done, how they sample and which laboratory they use, rather than relying on a title.

When to bring one in. Recommend an independent assessment when occupants report health problems or when you cannot work out how far the contamination goes. On a Level 3 job add these: sensitive occupants such as patients, aged care residents or young children; a contaminated air-conditioning system; a large loss across several areas; a dispute or a likely claim; and any client, insurer or school system that requires sampling. When in doubt, recommend one in writing and let the client decide.Why the clearance must be independent. The company that did the work has an interest in the work passing. If the same company sets the pass mark, takes the samples and reads the results, nobody else can trust the outcome, and you have nothing to stand on if it is challenged later. The answer to the builder in Toowoomba is a polite no: you will do your own post-remediation evaluation, and an independent hygienist will do the verification.Writing the brief. A good brief saves days. It tells the hygienist what happened and asks the questions you need answered. Include the building, its age and use, and who occupies it; the water event and the dates; what you have found so far, with photos and moisture maps; the areas in and out of scope; and the questions, for example \"Is the air-conditioning serving Rooms 4 and 5 affected?\" or \"What will the pass criteria be?\". Ask for the pass criteria in writing before you start, the sampling plan, the laboratory and its accreditation, how long results take and who receives the report. Add site safety: the hygienist enters your work area under your SWMS, so they need an induction and the right respirator.

Keep the roles clean. The hygienist assesses and verifies. You scope the work and carry it out. If the hygienist's report recommends something you disagree with, raise it in writing with your evidence. Do not change their findings in your own report.

See it

Do it in metric

Put the scope in the brief in numbers. Classroom 4 is 8.4 m \u00d7 7.2 m = 60.5 m\u00b2 of floor; Classroom 5 is the same, 60.5 m\u00b2. The corridor outside both is 2.4 m \u00d7 16.0 m = 38.4 m\u00b2.

Area for the hygienist to assess = 60.5 + 60.5 + 38.4 = 159.4 m\u00b2. The ceiling is 2.7 m, so the volume of air in scope = 159.4 \u00d7 2.7 = 430 m\u00b3.

Add the moisture readings in the same units you will report at the end: the plasterboard behind the joinery read 38% WME against a dry reference of 12% WME in the same wall.

Field download: Brief for an occupational hygienist

Use this on site and file it with the job record.

  • Building: address, age, construction, use, who occupies it (and anyone vulnerable).
  • Event: water source, dates, how long materials were wet, what has been done so far.
  • Findings so far: photos, moisture map, areas of visible growth with m\u00b2 estimates.
  • Areas in scope and out of scope, with floor areas in m\u00b2 and a plan.
  • Questions to answer (for example: extent of Condition 2, HVAC involvement, reoccupation).
  • Pass criteria to be agreed in writing before work starts.
  • Sampling plan, laboratory name and accreditation, turnaround time.
  • Independence: any link with the remediator, insurer or builder disclosed in writing.
  • Site safety for entry to work areas: induction, SWMS, respirator, PPE.
  • Who pays, who receives the report, and the date it is needed.

Download the brief for an occupational hygienist

Check yourself

The Module 5 check asks these three questions about this lesson. Answer them in your head now, then test your reasoning in the check. Each answer comes with an explanation.

  1. Name two situations on a Level 3 job where you would recommend an independent hygienist.
  2. Why should the company that did the remediation not also confirm the clearance?
  3. When should the pass criteria be agreed, and with whom?

Takeaway

Bring in an independent hygienist early, brief them in writing and agree the pass criteria before you start. You do your own check; they confirm the clearance. Next: what sampling can and cannot tell you.

",
